entry.title: Annoyances
entry.summary: The small stuff, in one drawer, with what to do about it and what to say afterwards. None of these will end your trip. Most of them will end up being the bit you tell people about.

entry.title: Chiang Mai to Pai
entry.summary: Route 107 north out of the city to the Route 1095 turn, then over the hills to Pai. The shortest leg of the circuit by distance and the one people most often underestimate by time.

entry.title: Hot to Chiang Mai
entry.summary: The commute home. Four to six lanes with a median, narrowing to two through the town centres.

entry.title: Khun Yuam to Mae Sariang
entry.summary: Ninety-odd kilometres of Route 108 that the Thai highway article describes as running parallel to the Yuam river.

entry.title: Mae Sariang to Hot
entry.summary: The emptiest stretch of the circuit. Sealed, two lanes, steep hillsides, few villages, and a national park in the middle.

entry.title: Mae Hong Son to Khun Yuam
entry.summary: Route 108 south. The climb out of the Mae Hong Son valley, then the first of the long southern running.

entry.title: Pai to Soppong
entry.summary: Short. Out of the Pai basin, up, and into limestone country.

entry.title: The Samoeng warm-up
entry.summary: Chiang Mai to Mae Rim, Route 1096 to Samoeng, and back. A day. Not part of the loop.

entry.title: Soppong to Mae Hong Son
entry.summary: Fifty-two kilometres, a hundred and ninety curves, and a long drop into the Mae Hong Son valley at the end.

entry.title: The 1263 cut
entry.summary: Khun Yuam east to Mae Chaem. Optional. A three-day loop instead of a four-day one, bought with the steepest and most curve-dense road here.

entry.title: Route 107
entry.summary: Chiang Mai north towards Fang. The loop uses only its first stretch, as far as the Route 1095 turn near Mae Malai.

entry.title: Route 108
entry.summary: Chiang Mai to Mae Hong Son the long way round: south through Hang Dong and Chom Thong to Hot, then west and north through Mae Sariang, Mae La Noi and Khun Yuam.

entry.title: Route 1088
entry.summary: North out of Mae Chaem. Relevant to this circuit only as part of the 1263 shortcut's eastern exit.

entry.title: Route 1095
entry.summary: Nong Khong on Route 107, over the hills to Pai, through Pangmapha, and down into Mae Hong Son. Sealed two lanes end to end. The most curve-dense long road on the circuit.

entry.title: Route 1096
entry.summary: Mae Rim to Samoeng, ridden as a day loop out of Chiang Mai and back. Not part of the Mae Hong Son circuit, and the best possible preparation for it.

entry.title: Route 1263
entry.summary: Khun Yuam east to Mae Chaem. The shortcut that halves the loop, and the hardest riding in this network.

entry.title: Chiang Mai
entry.summary: The start and the finish. Both roads out of it — 107 to the north, 108 to the south — are the loop's two ends.

entry.title: Hot
entry.summary: The hinge of the southern leg: east of here Route 108 is four to six lanes to Chiang Mai, west of here it is two lanes for 265 kilometres.

entry.title: Khun Yuam
entry.summary: On Route 108 between Mae Hong Son and Mae La Noi, and the western end of the 1263 cut to Mae Chaem. Two reasons to stop, and both of them are specific.

entry.title: Mae Chaem
entry.summary: A Chiang Mai district in its own valley, reached from the loop only by Route 1263 or over the Inthanon massif.

entry.title: Mae Hong Son
entry.summary: The far end of the loop and the only town on it with an airport, a hospital of size, and a chedi on a hill above the runway. Population small, altitude low, mountains on every side.

entry.title: Mae Sariang
entry.summary: The largest town on the southern leg and the natural overnight between Mae Hong Son and Chiang Mai. Teak-era shophouses, Burmese-style wats, and a river.

entry.title: Pai
entry.summary: Night one clockwise. A small district town in a flat river basin ringed by hills, with more guesthouses, coffee and motorcycle rental per head than anywhere else on the circuit.

entry.title: Soppong
entry.summary: The main settlement of Pang Mapha district, in limestone karst country. Officially Pang Mapha; on the road signs and in every conversation, Soppong.

entry.title: Ban Rak Thai
entry.summary: A village north of Mae Hong Son settled by Chinese Yunnanese, on a reservoir, with tea terraces and the border immediately behind it.

entry.title: Doi Inthanon
entry.summary: 2,565 metres, in Chom Thong district, reached from Route 108 or from Mae Chaem over Route 1088. Not on the loop; one turn off it.

entry.title: Huai Nam Dang
entry.summary: A national park straddling the Chiang Mai and Mae Hong Son line, right on Route 1095, with a viewpoint that looks east over cloud at dawn.

entry.title: The Japanese memorial at Khun Yuam
entry.summary: A memorial hall in Khun Yuam holding material from the Japanese presence in this district during the Second World War.

entry.title: Mae Sam Laep and the Salween
entry.summary: A river village west of Mae Sariang at the end of a side road, on the Salween where it forms the frontier.

entry.title: Mae Surin Waterfall
entry.summary: A single-drop waterfall in Namtok Mae Surin National Park, in Khun Yuam district.

entry.title: Op Luang
entry.summary: A gorge on the Chaem river in a national park on Route 108, roughly midway between Hot and Mae Sariang.

entry.title: Pa Bong Piang rice terraces
entry.summary: In Mae Chaem district, off the eastern end of the 1263 cut. One of the reasons to take the shortcut at all.

entry.title: Pai Canyon
entry.summary: Kong Lan: narrow eroded sandstone ridges on the edge of the Pai basin, walked at sunset by most of the town.

entry.title: The evening in Pai
entry.summary: Pai's evening market runs down the main street every night in the season: food stalls, music, and most of the town's visitors in one place.

entry.title: Pang Ung
entry.summary: A royal-project reservoir in the hills north-west of Mae Hong Son, reached by the same road system as Ban Rak Thai.

entry.title: Su Tong Pae bridge
entry.summary: A long bamboo bridge over rice fields and a stream outside Mae Hong Son town, on the route toward Khun Yuam.

entry.title: Tham Lot
entry.summary: A limestone cave in Pang Mapha district with the Nam Lang stream running through it. Entered by lamp and by bamboo raft, with a local guide.

entry.title: Tham Pla, the fish cave
entry.summary: A spring-fed pool at a cave mouth north of Mae Hong Son town, in its own national park, holding a resident population of large barb.

entry.title: Wat Chong Kham and Wat Chong Klang
entry.summary: The pair of Shan-Burmese temples on Nong Chong Kham, the pond at the centre of Mae Hong Son town.

entry.title: Wat Phra That Doi Kong Mu
entry.summary: The temple on the hill west of Mae Hong Son town. Two Shan-style chedis, a road to the top, and the view that gives the province its nickname.
